Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.

Article continues below this ad
Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Your endorsement of Scott Wiener deserves a closer examination of the philosophy behind his housing and wealth policies.
Unequal wealth is a fact; it does not, by itself, establish an injustice or a government duty to reduce it. People build wealth through work, saving, investment, entrepreneurship, risk and circumstance. Wiener’s policies reflect a different premise: that disparities in wealth and access to affluent communities are problems government should correct through taxation and housing policy. His housing policies use state authority to require communities—including affluent, low-density communities—to accommodate housing across income levels, with consequences for noncompliance. This shifts important land-use decisions from local communities to the state.Meanwhile, many Californians earn too much for substantial assistance but too little to buy homes in expensive communities. Policy should focus on upward mobility—better schools, safer communities, etc. - not simply equal $$
Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.
One thing the measure doesn’t fully account for: upkeep. As the Chronicle has rigorously documented (https://www.sfchronicle.com/projects/2022/san-francisco-sros/), many deed-restricted affordable homes in places like San Francisco are deteriorating. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.
This is a fundamental problem with California’s focus on 100% affordable housing developments — rents don’t cover the bills, necessitating significant ongoing subsidies.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.
Wicks told us California also needs to restructure its budgets to establish “sustained ongoing funding for affordable housing so that we’re not having to have this bond conversation every six years.”

What does California Proposition 1 do?
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Supporters
Arguments for
California needs more money for housing in order to help the state’s more than 180,000 homeless residents, as well as those who pay more than they can afford in rent and those who can’t afford to purchase a home.

Arguments against
Some Republican legislators criticized the bill for using veterans to drum up support while actually doing little to serve them. They also questioned the wisdom of borrowing more money to pay for housing without addressing the underlying reasons it’s so expensive to build.

Props. 1 and 38 would take the state deeper in debt for uncertain gains
Two measures on the November ballot ask voters to borrow $20 billion combined. Proposition 1 would fund housing programs. Proposition 38 would fund immunology research. We recommend a no vote on each.
The state already carries a heavy debt load. California owed about $70 billion on general obligation bonds as of Sept. 1, according to the state treasurer. Voters and lawmakers have authorized nearly $38 billion more in bonds that have not yet been sold.
The bondholders who lent the state money expect to be paid back with interest. The state spends about $6 billion annually from the general fund repaying bonds. Props. 1 and 38 would add roughly $1 billion to that for 20 to 25 years.
When state revenue comes up short, lawmakers can reduce spending or at least slow spending growth. Bond payments, however, are a legal obligation that comes due regardless. Every dollar locked into debt service is a taxpayer dollar unavailable for schools, health care or wildfire protection in a lean year.
Prop. 1: Housing money without accountability
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
Most of the money, about $7.2 billion, would pay for building, buying and rehabilitating multifamily rental housing, affordable housing and supportive housing for the homeless. Smaller pools of money totaling about $2.3 billion would provide mortgage and down-payment assistance.
Giving buyers more money with which to bid without adding homes would push prices higher. And buying existing apartments does not add a single home to ease market pressure.
The measure also lacks accountability. It calls for an annual report on how well things are going, but there is no independent audit on most of it and no remedy if the return on investment is lackluster. There also are no plans for when the money runs out and no guarantee that lawmakers will not meddle and reapportion the funds.
Californians have cause for skepticism that the state will spend this housing money well. A 2024 state audit found that California had not consistently tracked whether its homelessness spending worked. Sacramento should prove that it can measure and deliver results before asking for bonds that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
Prop. 38: Science by ballot box
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. Only one University of California-affiliated institute appears to qualify for half of the money, according to a CalMatters analysis. Coincidentally, that institute’s co-founder is one of Prop. 38’s biggest backers.
One problem with this approach is that state law would lock in how the money could be spent. Research dollars should support the centers with the most promising results and best scientists. Maybe that is the UC affiliate now, but that could change.
Bonds also fit research poorly. They are better suited to bridges and schools that last decades than to research that might never bear fruit. Even if there are commercial breakthroughs, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says royalties could take decades to repay the bonds, if they ever do.
Medical research is a legitimate state interest. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.

Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).

How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.

The funding approved by voters through the 2018 Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond Act has been fully committed — exhausted within five years, by the end of 2023, due to overwhelming demand. The state’s flagship Multifamily Housing Program, which relied on funding from the bond and one-time General Fund investments, is routinely oversubscribed by roughly 9 to 1. Together these signal that the barrier to building more affordable housing in California isn’t a lack of will or projects — it’s a lack of sustainable funding.
Without new state investments, affordable housing production will stall just as California is making meaningful progress and as federal cuts threaten to make it even more difficult for Californians to make ends meet, which is why state lawmakers placed Prop. 1 on the ballot.
What Affordable Housing and Homeownership Programs Would Prop. 1 Fund?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize $11.25 billion in general obligation (GO) bonds that would support the construction and preservation of affordable rental homes, expand homeownership assistance for low- and moderate-income homebuyers, including veterans, and provide permanent housing for people at risk of or experiencing homelessness. Within these categories, it would provide some funding for programs that serve distinct populations, such as California tribes, farmworkers, unhoused youth, and college students. The bond funds would be allocated as follows:
Affordable Housing Development and Preservation
$5.1 billion for the Multifamily Housing Program (MHP) , which supports the construction, rehabilitation, or preservation of affordable rental housing. At least 10% of units in a MHP development must be available for extremely low-income households who are at the highest risk of facing homelessness. This is one of California’s model affordable housing development programs.
$1.15 billion for supportive housing through the MHP program. Supportive housing provides stable homes with wrap-around services for people who were chronically homeless or at risk of becoming so. These funds can be used for operating subsidy reserves, which are critical to the longevity and sustainability of permanent supportive housing.
Up to 15% — $150 million — would be allocated as grants to acquire or build permanent supportive housing among other specified uses.
Another $150 million is carved out for the capital development or acquisition of youth housing through MHP. This would serve current or former foster youth, homeless minors or youth, or youth at risk of homelessness.
$750 million for the Portfolio Reinvestment Program, which provides funding to rehabilitate and extend the long-term affordability of state-funded rental multifamily housing projects that are at risk of conversion to market-rate housing.
$500 million for the Infill Infrastructure Grant Program . This would provide incentive grants to assist with new construction and rehabilitation of infrastructure that supports high-density affordable and mixed-income housing in locations designated as infill.
$450 million for the Joe Serna, Jr. Farmworker Housing Program to fund grants or loans for the construction or rehabilitation of housing for agricultural employees and their families.
$350 million for affordable student housing projects to be split evenly between the University of California and the California State University.
$200 million for a new Community Anti-Displacement and Preservation Program, which helps protect unsubsidized housing that may naturally be affordable and requires long-term affordability regulations.
$200 million for the Tribal Housing Grant Program which finances housing and housing-related activities to enable tribes to rebuild and reconstitute their communities.
$200 million to the Affordable Housing Innovation Fund for the Local Housing Trust Fund Matching Grant Program. This would fund competitive grants or loans to local housing trust funds that develop, own, lend, or invest in affordable housing and would be used to create pilot programs to demonstrate innovative approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.
Homeownership
$1.25 billion for the CalVet Home Loan Program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans) to help veterans and their families purchase homes. This portion of the bond would be repaid through mortgage (principal and interest) payments.
$600 million for the CalHome program. CalHome provides forgivable loans for lower-income households in self-help homeownership projects, including subdivisions and manufactured homes.
$500 million for the My Home downpayment assistance program to fund low-to-moderate income home purchase assistance programs.
What Benefits Would Prop. 1 Create for California’s Economy & Communities?
Prop. 1 would help expand and preserve California’s affordable housing supply while generating economic benefits and advancing the state’s housing goals. The bond would help close the financing gap for affordable rental homes, which serve lower-income California families and include seniors, people with disabilities, farmworkers, college students, and unhoused youth. According to legislative analyses (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), the bond is expected to:
Produce more than 40,000 new affordable homes for lower-income families and individuals.
Preserve more than 5,500 existing affordable homes , ensuring they remain affordable for future generations.
Create more than 53,000 construction jobs through building new housing across the state.
Generate $1.3 billion in state and local tax revenue that supports local communities and public services.
Every $1 invested in state affordable housing leverages roughly $4 (https://roadmaphome.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/Roadmap-Home-Report-2026.pdf) in federal, local, and private investment, maximizing the impact of public dollars. Affordable housing also delivers economic, health, and environmental benefits (https://affordablehomes.calhousingpartnership.org/). For example:
Children who grow up in affordable housing earn a median of $51,000 more over their lifetimes,
Permanent supportive housing saves an estimated $1.80 in public costs for every $1 invested (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8863642/pdf/nihms-1768403.pdf), and
Building homes near jobs and transit lowers transportation costs while reducing greenhouse gas emissions (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/policy-and-research/intersectional-policy-work/housing-and-climate-change).
Together, these investments would expand housing opportunities, reduce housing instability, strengthen local economies, and help California meet its long-term housing needs.
How Would Prop. 1 Be Repaid?
Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a total of $11.25 billion in GO bonds, divided as follows:
A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.

A $10 billion GO bond for affordable housing and homeownership programs that would be repaid from the state’s General Fund, and
A $1.25 billion veterans’ bond, a type of tax-exempt GO bond, for the CalVet Home Loan program that would be repaid through mortgage payments, with the General Fund as a backstop.
California voters often pass GO bonds to fund infrastructure projects that are designed to serve the public over many generations, as has been the case with affordable housing. Voters have also historically passed veterans’ bonds for CalVet to support homeownership opportunities for veterans.
GO bonds are repaid from the state’s General Fund. Repaying the $10 billion bond would cost $580 million per year for the next 30 years, for a total estimated cost of $17.4 billion ($10 billion in principal and $7.39 billion in interest). As of the governor’s proposed 2026-27 budget, California had $6.3 billion in General Fund debt service for GO bonds, or roughly 2.6% of General Fund expenditures.
In contrast, veterans bonds are generally self-supporting because they are repaid through principal and interest payments made by CalVet Home Loan Program borrowers. However, they are still GO bonds and are ultimately backed by the state’s General Fund. If program revenues were insufficient to cover the debt service, the General Fund would be responsible for the difference. It is unclear how often, if ever, the General Fund has had to backfill debt payments for previous veterans bonds.
Prop. 1 bond dollars would replenish depleted affordable housing programs. But bond dollars alone will not solve the housing shortage, nor would they replace the need for ongoing investments to meet the state’s substantial housing needs.
Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 Draw From Same Bonding Capacity, Face Important Trade Offs
Voters face two GO bond measures on the November 2026 ballot: Prop. 1 and Proposition 38. Prop. 38 would authorize $8.4 billion in GO bonds to support research and development in immunology and immunotherapy. Voters should weigh how each proposal addresses the state’s most pressing needs, fits within California’s limited borrowing capacity, and affects the state’s ability to invest in services that help families today and in the future.
Like all GO bonds, Prop. 38 would require long-term General Fund debt-service payments — estimated at $500 million annually (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) for 25 years — reducing budget and bonding capacity for other state priorities. If both Prop. 1 and Prop. 38 are approved, it would reduce General Fund dollars by roughly $1.1 billion annually.
Public sector investment in scientific research is needed, particularly given federal cuts, but Prop. 38 raises important fiscal and policy considerations. GO bonds are conventionally used to finance infrastructure projects — like roads, bridges, or housing — that can be used over decades, roughly matching the time it takes to repay the bond itself.
Funding research through GO bonds does not work the same way. Bond-funded research gets most of the dollars upfront for grants, salaries, and operating costs, but are not guaranteed to be built into a lasting asset. Research findings do compound overtime, but the bond dollars themselves are depleted after a few years. The state then spends years or decades paying interest on bonds that stopped directly funding work long ago. So while scientific research needs funding, a GO bond is not the appropriate funding mechanism. Plus, half of Prop. 38’s funding would be concentrated on a limited set of health conditions, even though California already has multiple public and private research institutions (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Initiative/2025-026) conducting work in these areas.
Prop. 1 doesn’t confront these same challenges. While previous affordable housing bond dollars were also used up quickly, they left behind affordable homes that will continue to serve numerous families for decades. Affordable housing developments that use state dollars must have affordability requirements for at least 55 years — way beyond the repayment of the bonds with which they’re financed. The community benefits and capital assets outlast the debt, which is the intended purpose of GO bonds.
Prop. 1 Supporters and Opponents
Prop. 1 is supported by a broad coalition (https://www.housingbondca.com/coalition) of organizations representing housing, business, labor, local government, older adults, tenants, homelessness, urban planning, construction, environmental, and civil rights interests, among others.
Official opposition has been limited. The primary opponents on record include a few Republican state legislators who voted against (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417) placing the measure on the ballot.

The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. The problem underlying California’s housing crisis comes down to this: the cost of construction.
It constrains new supply. And the only way to recoup the costs of what does get built requires high rents and mortgages or — in the case of affordable housing — public subsidies.
Unfortunately, the solution to this crisis offered by two statewide propositions has nothing to do with addressing prohibitive building costs. Instead, their answer is to load Californians with debt while delivering bonanzas to home developers and builders.

Proposition 1 leaves taxpayers indebted; Proposition 37, homebuyers.
Reject both.
Proposition 1
This measure, placed on the ballot by the state Legislature through Senate Bill 407, is an expensive pandering potpourri of giveaways. Veterans, farmworkers, students, tribes are all the ostensible beneficiaries.
Here’s how it is supposed to work:
Proposition 1 would authorize the state to sell $11.25 billion in general obligation bonds, all earmarked for various housing programs. The bulk of the bonds, $7.2 billion, would be spent acquiring, building or renovating apartments. The backers of this proposition optimistically estimate that it would subsidize the construction of “up to” 40,000 multifamily rental units as well as 2,500 housing units for farmworkers and 1,200 beds for university students.
Another $1.1 billion would provide homeownership assistance for 40,000 families. The remainder of funds would go toward infrastructure projects ($500 million), farmworker housing ($450 million), student housing at the UC and Cal State systems ($350 million), and tribal housing ($200 million).
Additionally, $1.25 billion would be dedicated to home loan assistance for veterans. (This program is not expected to create direct costs as participating veterans would pay monthly payments to the state, according to the Legislative Analyst’s Office.)
The need for affordable housing and housing assistance in this state is undeniable. More than two in five households spend, at least, 30% of their incomes on housing.
However, Proposition 1 would only provide a drop in the bucket towards adding to the state’s housing supply, all while hamstringing state spending and burdening taxpayers with decades of debt. The LAO projects that paying off $10 billion in bond debt incurred by this measure would require annual payments between $500 million to $600 million for a quarter of a century. These payments would come from California’s checking account, the General Fund. Because the state has to pay interest on the money it borrows, per the LAO, the total cost of the bond would be about 15% more (after adjusting for inflation) than if the state paid up front with money it already has.
Perhaps that would be acceptable if this burst of spending would make a long-term difference, but it’s doubtful.
Consider that California needs to build 2.5 million new homes, including 1 million affordable ones, to keep up with demand.
But this measure would add only 4% toward the affordable total, and that’s only under pie-in-the-sky circumstances.
More disconcerting is how this measure would do nothing to attack the root of the affordable housing cost problem:
Building subsidized housing in California costs 1.5 times the average cost of building already-exorbitant market-rate housing here, according to a 2025 RAND study.
The nonpartisan think tank identified two major reasons for the discrepancy: Local governments charge “unusually large” architectural and engineering fees, and they require that affordable housing developers pay “substantially above-market” wages.
While $200 million of Proposition 1 would go toward “pilot” programs aimed at developing reduced housing models, at least $10 billion would be spent keeping this bloated model afloat.
Proposition 37
This measure looks great on the surface. It would help Californians buy new homes, all without costing taxpayers a dime.
Well, all that glitters isn’t gold.
Proposition 37 would authorize up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for downpayment assistance on newly constructed homes. Eligible buyers could borrow up to 17% of a home’s purchase price through a fixed-rate second mortgage, making a down payment as low as 3%.
For example, consider an $800,000 home. A buyer could put down $24,000, borrow $136,000 through Proposition 37 and then finance the remaining $640,000 using a conventional mortgage.
A 30-year loan at today’s rates would make the monthly costs of that second mortgage more than $900.
Proposition 37 is not reducing the burden of home prices in California.
It’s not solving the affordability crisis.
It’s just a creative way to help Californians take on more debt.
What rightly worries critics is the terms of these additional loans. When borrowers default, the primary mortgage lender gets repaid first, meaning that the owner of the secondary takes on more risk. That would almost certainly mean that investors would require that buyers pay higher rates on their second mortgages than they pay on the first.
The LAO identifies these financing terms and investor participation as significant uncertainties.
Proposition 37 does nothing to address the main obstacle to homeownership in the state: the monthly cost of a conventional mortgage.
While the majority of renters in the state have incomes that would make them eligible to benefit from the measure’s secondary mortgage program, many wouldn’t qualify for a conventional mortgage in the first place even with its down payment assistance, according to the Public Policy Institute of California.
Far from solving the problem of high home prices, Proposition 37 could compound it.
While the measure restricts using the downpayment assistance to previously unpurchased homes, that does not mean that Proposition 37 will unleash a large new supply of housing.
What’s infinitely more probable is that Proposition 37 would expand purchasing power faster than it would induce new construction — and therefore push up prices.
Homes in California, especially new ones, are sitting unsold longer. In fact, builders have created a glut of new housing in the Central Valley they can’t sell, a dynamic exacerbated as interest rates have climbed. In fact, this summer Fresno topped Realtor.com’s list of U.S. cities with the highest share of new home listings (68%) cutting prices. Builders in the region, like Lennar, are reportedly panicking and responding by offering steeper discounts to lure buyers.

Endorsement: Affordable housing in California isn’t going to pay for itself. Is Prop 1 the answer?
Proposition 1 would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand opportunities for owning a home.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 26, 2026
The housing debate in California often feels a bit like fighting with your rambling uncle during Thanksgiving dinner. But there’s generally one island of universal agreement in a sea of rage: the need for more affordable housing.
A recent legislative analysis found (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-04/ahcd-hearing-packet-for-the-website.pdf) that 2.2 million extremely low-income and low-income California households are competing for just 664,000 affordable rental homes. To even come close to meeting demand, the California Department of Housing and Community Development estimated the state needs at least 1 million new affordable units by 2031, (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/sites/default/files/docs/policy-and-research/plan-report/StateofCADraft-2022-2023-AAP-12-6-22.pdf) including about 47,000 in San Francisco (https://sfgov.legistar.com/View.ashx?GUID=EDE50759-96D2-4873-846C-70851EEE4957&ID=15560084&M=F&).
Building this level of subsidized affordable housing will be neither easy nor cheap — and there’s lots of competition for limited funds.
In 2018, voters approved $4 billion in bonds for affordable and veteran housing (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=1&year=2018), all of which was allocated by the end of 2023. California’s Multifamily Housing Program (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/funding/mhp) — the state’s primary vehicle for providing developers with low-cost loans to build, rehabilitate and preserve affordable housing — has $9 in requests for every dollar available, a California Budget and Policy Center analysis found (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-1-californias-veterans-and-affordable-housing-bond/).

Proposition 1 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop1-text-proposed-laws.pdf), which the state Legislature placed on the November ballot with bipartisan support (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billVotesClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417), would authorize California to issue $11.25 billion in new bonds to create and preserve affordable housing and expand homeownership opportunities. Befitting the broad consensus on the state’s affordability crisis, it has no formal opposition.
The measure is rigidly prescriptive in its allocation of funds.
It allocates $7.2 billion to the Multifamily Housing Program — which the measure’s author, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, described in an endorsement interview as the “workhorse” of California’s efforts to develop affordable rental homes. Of that pool, $1.15 billion would be reserved for supportive housing and services for people at risk of or exiting homelessness, with $150 million set aside for youth who are homeless or in foster care. Another $750 million would go to renovating and modernizing existing affordable housing.

Outside of that bucket, $1.25 billion is earmarked for the CalVet Home Loan program (https://www.calvet.ca.gov/HomeLoans), which uses the proceeds from bond sales to provide loans to veterans to purchase homes. This program doesn’t cost taxpayers anything because veterans repay the cost of the bonds and interest through their loan payments. (Some Republican lawmakers accused Democrats of trying to inflate voter support for the measure by calling it the Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond when only about 10% of the overall funds go to veterans.)
Another $600 million would go to local agencies and nonprofits — such as Habitat for Humanity — to work with would-be homeowners to build or finance affordable homes, while $500 million would go to down-payment assistance for eligible first-time home buyers.
Among the measure’s other earmarks: $500 million for developing infrastructure — such as water and sewage lines — to support affordable housing, $450 million to build and rehabilitate farmworker housing, $350 million to be split evenly between the University of California and California State University systems for student housing, $200 million to tribal housing programs and $200 million to local grants and pilot programs that “demonstrate innovative, cost-saving approaches to creating or preserving affordable housing.”
If this seems like a dizzying array of priorities, that’s because it is.

Prop 1 is the product of years of legislative sausage-making: It combines bits and pieces of policies proposed by lawmakers and advocates, each with a specific group or issue they’re trying to address.

So, is the measure too unwieldy — and divided among too many different groups and interests — to be effective?
Wicks told us she is “very aware of that concern” but emphasized that each of the programs receiving funding in the bond is “a proven model that we know works.”
Altogether, Prop 1 could subsidize the creation of as many as 40,000 affordable rental units, plus 2,500 for farmworkers and another 1,200 for college students, according to estimates from the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop1-110326.pdf) — while helping 40,000 households, including 2,100 veterans, achieve homeownership. (A separate November ballot measure, Prop 37 (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/prop-37-housing-home-loans-22422795.php), would provide down-payment assistance to middle-income Californians, at no cost to taxpayers.)
This, of course, is a drop in the bucket of California’s housing needs — at a not insignificant cost. The state will need to make estimated annual payments of $500 million to $600 million from the general fund for 25 years to pay off the bond — 15% more expensive than an upfront payment. This will also reduce the money available for other critical programs at a time when California faces years of projected future budget deficits (https://lao.ca.gov/Publications/Report/5101).
But there is good reason to believe that California will, as Wicks put it, “have a better ROI on these resources today” than in the past.

That’s because the state has in recent years significantly reduced the roadblocks that delay housing and drive up the cost of production — including by exempting all infill development from unnecessary review (https://www.sfchronicle.com/california/article/ceqa-housing-roadblocks-newsom-20402835.php) under the California Environmental Quality Act and streamlining dense housing near transit (https://www.sfchronicle.com/bayarea/article/housing-transit-map-yimby-21075831.php).
Ongoing efforts to streamline the state’s maze of affordable housing financing programs (https://lao.ca.gov/publications/report/5199) into one consolidated application (https://ahcd.assembly.ca.gov/system/files/2026-08/ab-519-july-2026-deliverable-7.1.26-final-afforable-housing-finance-workgroup.pdf), along with other reforms, could also slash development costs by $60,000 to $70,000 per unit (https://www.hcd.ca.gov/about-hcd/newsroom/more-housing-faster-governor-newsom-signs-historic-housing-affordability-reforms).
“We’re at a great moment in time to actually have the best impact on housing that I’ve seen in my career,” Ray Pearl, executive director of the California Housing Consortium, told us.

(https://www.sfchronicle.com/sf/article/affordable-housing-sale-21251741.php) Prop 1 only sets aside a relative pittance for rehabilitation.

Legislators would be wise to pursue other paths, such as Washington state’s tax incentives (https://www.theurbanist.org/state-senate-greenlights-sweeping-tod-housing-bill/) to build affordable units inside market-rate developments, to share the burden of upkeep with the private sector.

Props. 1 and 38 would take the state deeper in debt for uncertain gains
Two measures on the November ballot ask voters to borrow $20 billion combined. Proposition 1 would fund housing programs. Proposition 38 would fund immunology research. We recommend a no vote on each.
The state already carries a heavy debt load. California owed about $70 billion on general obligation bonds as of Sept. 1, according to the state treasurer. Voters and lawmakers have authorized nearly $38 billion more in bonds that have not yet been sold.
The bondholders who lent the state money expect to be paid back with interest. The state spends about $6 billion annually from the general fund repaying bonds. Props. 1 and 38 would add roughly $1 billion to that for 20 to 25 years.
When state revenue comes up short, lawmakers can reduce spending or at least slow spending growth. Bond payments, however, are a legal obligation that comes due regardless. Every dollar locked into debt service is a taxpayer dollar unavailable for schools, health care or wildfire protection in a lean year.
Prop. 1: Housing money without accountability
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
Most of the money, about $7.2 billion, would pay for building, buying and rehabilitating multifamily rental housing, affordable housing and supportive housing for the homeless. Smaller pools of money totaling about $2.3 billion would provide mortgage and down-payment assistance.
Giving buyers more money with which to bid without adding homes would push prices higher. And buying existing apartments does not add a single home to ease market pressure.
The measure also lacks accountability. It calls for an annual report on how well things are going, but there is no independent audit on most of it and no remedy if the return on investment is lackluster. There also are no plans for when the money runs out and no guarantee that lawmakers will not meddle and reapportion the funds.
Californians have cause for skepticism that the state will spend this housing money well. A 2024 state audit found that California had not consistently tracked whether its homelessness spending worked. Sacramento should prove that it can measure and deliver results before asking for bonds that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
Prop. 38: Science by ballot box
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. Only one University of California-affiliated institute appears to qualify for half of the money, according to a CalMatters analysis. Coincidentally, that institute’s co-founder is one of Prop. 38’s biggest backers.
One problem with this approach is that state law would lock in how the money could be spent. Research dollars should support the centers with the most promising results and best scientists. Maybe that is the UC affiliate now, but that could change.
Bonds also fit research poorly. They are better suited to bridges and schools that last decades than to research that might never bear fruit. Even if there are commercial breakthroughs, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says royalties could take decades to repay the bonds, if they ever do.
Medical research is a legitimate state interest. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.

Props. 1 and 38 would take the state deeper in debt for uncertain gains
Two measures on the November ballot ask voters to borrow $20 billion combined. Proposition 1 would fund housing programs. Proposition 38 would fund immunology research. We recommend a no vote on each.
The state already carries a heavy debt load. California owed about $70 billion on general obligation bonds as of Sept. 1, according to the state treasurer. Voters and lawmakers have authorized nearly $38 billion more in bonds that have not yet been sold.
The bondholders who lent the state money expect to be paid back with interest. The state spends about $6 billion annually from the general fund repaying bonds. Props. 1 and 38 would add roughly $1 billion to that for 20 to 25 years.
When state revenue comes up short, lawmakers can reduce spending or at least slow spending growth. Bond payments, however, are a legal obligation that comes due regardless. Every dollar locked into debt service is a taxpayer dollar unavailable for schools, health care or wildfire protection in a lean year.
Prop. 1: Housing money without accountability
California needs more housing, and Prop. 1 would throw $11.25 billion at the problem without addressing the underlying causes of the state’s housing shortage and high costs. Lawmakers took the easy route. Rather than pass controversial reforms or find money in the budget, they chose to ask voters to borrow.
Most of the money, about $7.2 billion, would pay for building, buying and rehabilitating multifamily rental housing, affordable housing and supportive housing for the homeless. Smaller pools of money totaling about $2.3 billion would provide mortgage and down-payment assistance.
Giving buyers more money with which to bid without adding homes would push prices higher. And buying existing apartments does not add a single home to ease market pressure.
The measure also lacks accountability. It calls for an annual report on how well things are going, but there is no independent audit on most of it and no remedy if the return on investment is lackluster. There also are no plans for when the money runs out and no guarantee that lawmakers will not meddle and reapportion the funds.
Californians have cause for skepticism that the state will spend this housing money well. A 2024 state audit found that California had not consistently tracked whether its homelessness spending worked. Sacramento should prove that it can measure and deliver results before asking for bonds that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.
Prop. 38: Science by ballot box
Immunology and immunotherapy hold real promise, but Prop. 38 is the wrong way to fund research into them. Only one University of California-affiliated institute appears to qualify for half of the money, according to a CalMatters analysis. Coincidentally, that institute’s co-founder is one of Prop. 38’s biggest backers.
One problem with this approach is that state law would lock in how the money could be spent. Research dollars should support the centers with the most promising results and best scientists. Maybe that is the UC affiliate now, but that could change.
Bonds also fit research poorly. They are better suited to bridges and schools that last decades than to research that might never bear fruit. Even if there are commercial breakthroughs, the Legislative Analyst’s Office says royalties could take decades to repay the bonds, if they ever do.
Medical research is a legitimate state interest. If California wants to fund it, the state ought to do so through the regular budget process, weighing its value against other state priorities, not with a special bond that will cost taxpayers $500 million to $600 million per year.

What does California Proposition 1 do?
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
California needs more money for housing in order to help the state’s more than 180,000 homeless residents, as well as those who pay more than they can afford in rent and those who can’t afford to purchase a home.

Arguments against

Proposition 1
Borrow $11.25 billion for housing
Prop. 1 would allow the state to sell $11.25 billion in bonds to fund various affordable housing programs. Of that total amount, $1.25 billion would go toward veteran housing, while the rest would fund rental homes, homeownership programs, farmworker housing, affordable student housing, tribal housing and more. The bond is expected to help fund up to 40,000 multifamily rental units, while also helping another 40,000 households buy a home. The California Legislature put this measure on the ballot.
Weigh the arguments.
Take our quizzes to learn more about each proposition.

Summary
Support
California needs more money for housing in order to help the state’s more than 180,000 homeless residents, as well as those who pay more than they can afford in rent and those who can’t afford to purchase a home.
Oppose
Some Republican legislators criticized the bill for using veterans to drum up support while actually doing little to serve them. They also questioned the wisdom of borrowing more money to pay for housing without addressing the underlying reasons it’s so expensive to build.

Proposition committees
These committees are primarily formed to campaign for or against a proposition. They must identify contributors who give $100 or more, or loan a committee money. There are no limits on how much contributors can give or loan. Contributors who had their loans repaid or forgiven are still included. We exclude contributors who gave less than $100 in total. Contributors who made loans as part or all of their total are identified with an asterisk (*).
For funding by industry, we used existing sources, traditional machine learning and large language models to help categorize contributors who gave $5,000 or more in total, with CalMatters journalists reviewing the results. We also categorized the donors of political action committees that contributed to a campaign and used the results to calculate which industries should be applied. Major donors include individuals who self-identified as retired, self-employed, unemployed, a homemaker or a student.

Outside spending
Separate from proposition committees, outside groups can pay for ads, mailers and other efforts to influence voters. They can’t coordinate that spending with proposition committees. There is no limit on how much they can spend.

Fiscal Impact: Increased state cost of $500 million to $600 million annually for about 25 years to repay the housing bond.

Proposition 1: California’s Veterans and Affordable Housing Bond
A $11.25 Billion Bond to Continue Building Affordable Homes for Californians
July 2026 | By Monica Davalos (https://calbudgetcenter.org/people/monica-davalos/)
Print Report
key takeaway
Proposition 1, appearing on the November 2026 ballot, would provide funding for affordable housing and accessible homeownership. Prop. 1 asks voters to authorize a $11.25 billion general obligation bond to fund programs that support the creation and preservation of affordable housing, expand homebuying opportunities for low- and moderate-income Californians and veterans, and invest in permanent solutions to solve homelessness. If Prop. 1 is approved, it would replenish funding for several successful state programs that have exhausted their resources. Prop. 1 was placed on the ballot by the Legislature through passage of Senate Bill 417 (2026) (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260SB417).

How Has California Expanded Affordable Housing & What Gaps Remain?
Over the past six years, California has nearly tripled (https://calhousingpartnership.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/CHP_2026-Housing-Needs-Report-FINAL.pdf) the number of new affordable homes it funds. Yet the state continues to face a severe shortage of affordable housing, particularly for Californians with the lowest incomes. California needs more than 2.5 million new homes, including at least 1 million homes that are affordable to lower-income households. Housing cost pressures fall hardest on California renters as nearly half pay unaffordable rents — a hardship that disproportionately impacts Black and Latinx renters with low incomes, older adults, mixed-status families, and people with disabilities.
Unlike market-rate or luxury housing, affordable housing projects typically cannot be built without subsidies because affordable rents do not generate enough revenue to cover development or operating costs. As a result, affordable housing projects rely on multiple funding streams to close financing gaps. Currently, more than 46,000 affordable homes across California (491 developments) (https://www.enterprisecommunity.org/sites/default/files/2024-04/State_Pipeline_2024_FINAL.pdf) are waiting for the last bit of state funding needed to break ground. Prop. 1 would provide funding for various programs that help bridge the financial gap to keep affordable housing construction moving.
Why Is Affordable Housing Funding Running Out & How Would Prop. 1 Help?
Despite the ongoing housing affordability challenges Californians are facing, state funding for affordable housing has largely disappeared. Over the past several years, affordable housing programs have relied on one-time General Fund investments (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/protecting-progress-state-housing-and-homelessness-funding-must-continue/) to supplement voter-approved housing bonds, but those investments have drastically declined. The 2026 Budget Act only includes one-time investments in two significant affordable housing programs: $500 million for state Low Income Housing Tax Credits and $200 million for the Multifamily Housing Program, effectively leaving multiple programs (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/first-look-understanding-the-governors-proposed-2026-27-california-budget/#h-proposed-budget-includes-no-new-state-funding-for-affordable-housing) without additional funds. Beyond these investments, there is no meaningful ongoing or one-time investment from the state General Fund for affordable housing development.
The state’s remaining modest affordable housing funding sources, including the Affordable Housing and Sustainable Communities Program (AHSC), funded through Cap-and-Invest; state and federal Low-Income Housing Tax Credits; and SB 2 planning funds are insufficient to meet the demand and often require additional funding to be fully leveraged. The AHSC program was expected to receive nearly $800 million per year for affordable housing, but recent changes by the California Air Resources Board put that funding at risk.
